raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old man with no known chronic illnesses presented to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) in Kingston, Jamaica, with a history of back pain and fever beginning eight days prior to his presentation. The fever lasted for two days and settled with the use of paracetamol. He then started to experience severe arthralgia, myalgia, and generalized muscle weakness which lasted for the first few days of his illness. He was seen by his primary care physician three days after the onset of symptoms and was admitted to a private hospital with a diagnosis of dengue fever. He reported that his platelet count at that time was 44,000/muL but remained asymptomatic, with no signs of bleeding, and was therefore discharged with a plan for followup as an outpatient. Two days later he noticed dark-coloured, then red urine and therefore returned to the private hospital and was subsequently referred to the UHWI for further management.
At the time of presentation, there were no reports of mucosal bleeding, skin haemorrhages, or haematochezia. There was no history of retro-orbital pain, neck stiffness, or photophobia. There were no other urinary symptoms and no history of nausea or vomiting. Of note, he gave no history of exposure to rats and he had not travelled recently. However, he did recall a neighbour having a diagnosis of dengue fever 1-2 weeks prior to the onset of his symptoms. 
On physical examination, he had normal vital signs with a temperature of 36.3 C. His cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and central nervous systems were all normal. Examination of the skin did not reveal any petechiae, purpurae, ecchymoses, or rash. There were no wet purpurae in his mouth and fundoscopy was negative for retinal haemorrhages. A tourniquet test was performed and was negative. Urinalysis revealed a pH of 7.5 and tested positive for blood with no other abnormalities. 
Investigations from the private hospital revealed an initial leukopaenia, neutropaenia, and thrombocytopaenia, verified by peripheral blood film. By the time of his presentation to the UHWI, his white blood cell count had normalized but the platelet count remained low at 49,000/muL. However, manual review of the peripheral blood film revealed a higher count of 100,000/muL. His initial urea, creatinine, electrolytes, and coagulation studies were normal and remained normal for the duration of his admission. Creatinine level was 63 mumol/L on admission and 82 mumol/L at discharge. Admission aspartate transaminase was 1841 U/L (normal 7-32 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase was 159 U/L (normal 10-70 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase was 5740 U/L (normal 105-200 U/L). These values declined steadily during the admission and eventually normalized by the time of discharge. His initial creatine phosphokinase (CPK) was 325,600 U/L (normal for a male 40-240 U/L). With early and aggressive treatment, this value decreased by about 30-50% every day until it was 2,463 U/L at the time of discharge (see Figure 1). Urine microscopy was negative for red blood cells, casts, or other abnormal urinary sediments, but urinary myoglobin was positive. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and leptospirosis were all negative. Laboratory tests for the dengue virus on day four of his illness revealed a positive test for the dengue virus antigen, non-structural protein 1 (NS1), and negative immunoglobulin M (IgM). Dengue IgM became positive on day eight and remained positive on day 14. 
In-hospital management included aggressive hydration with intravenous and oral fluids, strict input/output charting, daily urinalyses to monitor pH, and close monitoring of the urea, creatinine, electrolytes, CPK, and platelet count. Target urine output was 200 mL/hour as recommended by Bosch and colleagues. Urinary pH remained above 6.0 throughout and therefore alkalinization of the urine with sodium bicarbonate was not instituted. The patient's hospital course was uncomplicated, he remained clinically well and was discharged with instructions to return initially for review on the ward and then for followup in the out-patient clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with dark, then red-colored urine following an 8-day history of back pain, fever, severe arthralgia, myalgia, and muscle weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with back pain and fever that began 8 days prior, lasted for 2 days, and settled with paracetamol. He then developed severe arthralgia, myalgia, and generalized muscle weakness. He was evaluated at a primary care clinic and admitted to a local hospital on day 3 with thrombocytopenia (platelet count 44,000/muL), but remained asymptomatic without bleeding and was discharged. Two days later, he noted dark-colored, followed by red-colored urine, prompting re-presentation and referral to the tertiary university hospital. He denied mucosal bleeding, skin hemorrhages, hematochezia, retro-orbital pain, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, or dysuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic illnesses. Denied recent travel or exposure to rats; noted an ill neighbor with an acute febrile illness 1-2 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dark/red urine, myalgias, arthralgias, back pain, and muscle weakness. Negative for mucosal bleeding, petechiae, hematochezia, retro-orbital pain, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, or vomiting. Home medications: paracetamol. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 36.3 C, vital signs normal. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and central nervous system examinations were normal. Skin examination showed no petechiae, purpurae, ecchymoses, or rash. Oral cavity showed no wet purpurae. Fundoscopy negative for retinal hemorrhages. Tourniquet test was negative.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count on arrival showed normalized white blood cell count and thrombocytopenia with platelet count 49,000/muL (manual peripheral blood film review: 100,000/muL; initial counts at prior facility: leukopenia, neutropenia, and platelets 44,000/muL). Serum creatinine: 63 mumol/L on admission, 82 mumol/L at discharge; urea, electrolytes, and coagulation studies normal throughout. AST: 1,841 U/L (reference: 7-32 U/L), GGT: 159 U/L (reference: 10-70 U/L), LDH: 5,740 U/L (reference: 105-200 U/L), declining to normal by discharge. Initial creatine phosphokinase (CPK): 325,600 U/L (reference: 40-240 U/L), declining to 2,463 U/L at discharge. Urinalysis: pH 7.5, positive for blood, negative for red blood cells, casts, or abnormal sediments; urine myoglobin: positive. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and leptospirosis were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue fever complicated by severe rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria without acute renal failure. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen on illness day 4 (IgM negative), with subsequent seroconversion to positive dengue IgM on day 8 and day 14. Leptospirosis, viral hepatitis (B and C), and HIV were excluded by negative serologies.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with aggressive hydration using intravenous and oral fluids targeting a urine output of 200 mL/hour, strict input/output charting, daily urine pH monitoring, and serial tracking of electrolytes, renal function, CPK, and platelets. Urine pH remained above 6.0, obviating the need for urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate. CPK declined by 30-50% daily, liver enzymes normalized, and the patient made an uneventful recovery and was discharged home with scheduled outpatient follow-up.
